summary: AE + SE walked the Acme Health Systems engineering team through Redwood SDK integration for Python and TypeScript, covering auth, env setup, quickstarts, and pointers for Dedicated/private deployment. Customer requested pricing, security docs, and a simple benchmark. Next steps and owners agreed.
transcript:
00:00 Alex (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, this is Alex from Redwood Inference, i think you all have Sam on the line too. Today we want to run through a short SDK integration walkthrough — Python and TypeScript quickstarts, auth, environment setup and next steps.
00:14 Jordan (Customer): Yep thanks Alex. I'm Jordan, CTO at Acme Health. Priya and Michael are on the call too. We mainly want to validate how fast our engineers can get a POC running, and what auth and data residency looks like.
00:28 Samir (SE): Great, i'll share my screen in a sec. Quick agenda: show the Python flow, the Node/TS flow, env vars and secrets (KMS notes), and then touch on Dedicated/private deployment considerations.
00:42 Priya (Customer): Quick Q — do we need a service account per microservice or can we reuse a single token across the app?
00:49 Samir (SE): Good question. For quickstarts we often use a single API key scoped to the project; for production we recommend per-service tokens with RBAC via SSO/SAML integrations and short-lived tokens from your vault.
01:02 Alex (AE): Also note we have audit logs and KMS integrations for private customers, that will be in the security pack we'll send.
01:12 Samir (SE): Ok sharing screen now — opening the repo: redwood-sdk-quickstart. Python first.
01:21 Samir (SE): In Python the install is pip install redwood-inference (sometimes shows redwood-sdk depending on pip index). Example snippet:
01:30 Samir (SE): from redwood import RedwoodClient
01:33 Samir (SE): client = RedwoodClient(api_key=os.getenv('REDWOOD_API_KEY'))
01:37 Samir (SE): response = client.generate("summarize: patient intake notes")
01:40 Priya (Customer): That looks straightforward. How do we handle region selection? We need EU-only processing for some PHI flows.
01:49 Samir (SE): You can set region in the client: RedwoodClient(region='eu-west-1') or via REDWOOD_REGION env var. For Private deployments you point the client at your private endpoint via REDWOOD_API_BASE.
02:02 Michael (Customer): Any pitfalls we should know about for KV cache or tokenization? We use long sequences for some clinical notes.
02:10 Samir (SE): For long sequences enable streaming and KV caching; note that transcription sometimes says KV "cash" — sorry, that's my note — but essentially our runtime handles KV cache across requests; you'll want to set max_sequence and also consider flashing to disk for very long contexts in private deployments.
02:26 Jordan (Customer): Does the SDK automatically batch requests? We might want to batch inference calls from our ingestion pipeline.
02:34 Samir (SE): SDK has a batching helper in runtimes for Python — you can configure batching window and max tokens. For high throughput we recommend Dedicated capacity with autoscaling policies.
02:44 Alex (AE): Quick aside — pricing vs latency tradeoffs, if you go Dedicated you get predictable latency and better throughput cost per token. Hosted is easier but can be more variable at scale.
02:58 Priya (Customer): Back to auth: is the REDWOOD_API_KEY a long-lived key? We want short-lived ideally.
03:05 Samir (SE): By default keys are long-lived but you can use our token exchange to mint short-lived tokens via your identity provider. We also support passing JWTs from your OIDC provider if you want per-request authorization.
03:20 Alex (AE): I'll include the token-exchange flow in the follow-up docs.
03:25 Samir (SE): Now TypeScript quickstart — npm install @redwood/inference (package name may vary in early builds). Example:
03:33 Samir (SE): import { RedwoodClient } from '@redwood/inference'
03:36 Samir (SE): const client = new RedwoodClient({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY, region: process.env.REDWOOD_REGION })
03:45 Samir (SE): const res = await client.generate({ model: 'redwood-4x', prompt: 'rewrite in plain english' })
03:52 Priya (Customer): Any differences in streaming between Node and Python?
03:55 Samir (SE): Same semantics, we expose an async iterator in Node and a callback/streaming API in Python. Occasionally the SDK names are slightly different in early versions, so check our package README.
04:10 Michael (Customer): We plan to run a small benchmark — maybe 50 QPS for a pilot. What should we expect?
04:18 Samir (SE): For hosted with a mid-tier model you might see p95 latencies around 200-400ms for single-turn gen at 512 tokens depending on batching; Dedicated with pinned GPUs will be lower and more predictable. We'll share a benchmark spreadsheet but you'll want to run the workload locally against our staging endpoint.
04:33 Jordan (Customer): You mentioned staging endpoints — is there a sandbox org?
04:36 Alex (AE): Yes we'll spin up a trial org and give you test credentials; Sam will provide a staging endpoint and the quickstart code to run a small bench.
04:44 Samir (SE): Now environment variables we typically use: REDWOOD_API_KEY, REDWOOD_REGION, REDWOOD_API_BASE (for private), REDWOOD_TIMEOUT_MS. For Docker containers we recommend mounting the key from your secret manager.
04:57 Priya (Customer): Got it. For private deployment, do we need to manage GPUs ourselves?
05:02 Samir (SE): For Redwood Private we provide an on-prem package — you can run on your infra or we can work with partners to provision. For Dedicated we manage GPU pools for you.
05:12 Alex (AE): Security checklist — SSO/SAML, RBAC, SOC2, ISO, KMS integration, audit logs. I'll attach our security pack in the follow up.
05:25 Priya (Customer): Anything special about CORS or client-side usage?
05:29 Samir (SE): We discourage embedding keys in browser clients; use a backend proxy to sign requests and stream to clients.
05:35 Jordan (Customer): What about cost controls — quotas or rate limits per team?
05:39 Alex (AE): We have per-key quotas, rate limits, and route-level caps. In Console you can set budgets and alerts. We'll show a quick Console view in a follow-up demo if helpful.
05:49 Samir (SE): Switching to a quick live demo — i'll run the Python quickstart locally.
06:00 Samir (SE): (typing) export REDWOOD_API_KEY=sk-test-REDACTED
06:05 Samir (SE): python quickstart.py
06:10 Samir (SE): output: streaming response starts... partial tokens... then final response: "Summary: patient reported mild headache, no fever, recommended follow-up" (note: example only).
06:28 Michael (Customer): The response looks clean. What about deterministic outputs across model versions? We need a pinned model for logs.
06:35 Samir (SE): You can pin model versions in the API call with model: 'redwood-4x@v1.2' or via route configs. Console shows version history and rollout controls.
06:46 Priya (Customer): Does the SDK log prompts locally? We worry about PII exfiltration.
06:50 Samir (SE): SDK does not log prompts by default; our runtime has redaction hooks and you can configure prompt masking client-side before sending. We'll share guidance.
07:03 Jordan (Customer): Do you support function calling or structured outputs? We have downstream parsers that expect JSON.
07:08 Samir (SE): Yes, we support structured output templates and function/tool calling. For TypeScript we show a typed interface example in the quickstart repo.
07:17 Priya (Customer): Any gotchas with tokenization when we serialize clinical data?
07:21 Samir (SE): Watch special characters and linebreaks; we recommend normalizing whitespace and using our tokenizer tool in the SDK for estimating tokens to control cost.
07:33 Alex (AE): Ok time check — about 25 minutes in. We'll wrap with next steps.
07:38 Samir (SE): Quick recap of code artifacts i'm sharing: python/quickstart.py, node/quickstart.ts, staging-bench.sh, token-estimator.py. Links i'll paste in chat.
07:48 Alex (AE): Next steps from the call: 1) Alex to send pricing + Dedicated options; 2) Samir to share quickstart snippets and staging endpoint; 3) Customer to provide QPS and infra diagram.
08:00 Jordan (Customer): Sounds good. Also can you include compliance and SOC2 stuff in the packet?
08:05 Alex (AE): Yup. We'll include SOC2 attestation, encryption docs, and data residency notes.
08:10 Priya (Customer): One more question — what is typical turnaround for a pilot?
08:14 Samir (SE): From our experience, a simple POC with test data can be up in 1-2 weeks; for Dedicated or Private it can take longer depending on procurement and network setup.
08:24 Michael (Customer): We'll aim for a 2-week pilot. We'll sync internally and get back to Alex.
08:29 Alex (AE): Great, i'll follow up with calendar invite for a kickoff once we share the trial org.
08:34 Jordan (Customer): Thanks everyone.
08:36 Alex (AE): Thanks all — end of call.

Note: Transcript has occasional ASR artifacts and slightly misattributed lines; see follow-up links for the exact quickstart code and staging endpoints.
